first_impression.reaction: My assistant flagged this because one side of a family we're close to is Yoruba and the question of a traditional day plus a white wedding has come up. The opening is calm and confident: "A Nigerian wedding begins long before the wedding day." She summarised it. I read the Yoruba section, the spraying section and the part about holding it abroad myself.

journey.section: What a traditional Nigerian wedding looks like today
journey.quote: The Yoruba are one of the three largest ethnic groups of Nigeria, concentrated in the south-west.
journey.reaction: Encyclopaedia opening. Anyone who would hire a planner for this already knows it. My assistant skipped the paragraph.
Why send me to Britannica? Then the V&A, then a journal paper. It reads like a school project, not a team that has stood in the room.

journey.section: 1. The introduction and the engagement ceremony
journey.quote: Families settle the list between themselves, and it varies widely.
journey.reaction: Right. No numbers, no assumptions about what a family brings. That's how it should be handled.

journey.quote: Aṣọ-òkè is a handmade strip-woven cloth historically produced by the Yoruba in south-western Nigeria, woven by men on a single-heddle loom in strips around four inches wide that are then stitched together.
journey.reaction: Loom widths. Too much. One line on why the cloth matters to the family would say more.

journey.section: 5. Kamu, when the bride is welcomed by the groom's family
journey.quote: Many families keep these gatherings for women only.
journey.reaction: Good. Shows they understand privacy around the women's side. That's the kind of cultural awareness I look for.

journey.quote: This [study of Igbo marriage stages](https://www.ijsshr.com/journal/index.php/IJSSHR/article/download/1147/987/3953) sets them out in full.
journey.reaction: A download link to an academic paper. I don't want homework. I want someone who knows.

journey.quote: Guests usually buy their own fabric from the family and arrange their own tailoring.
journey.reaction: For 300 guests across Dubai, London and Sydney, this is exactly what I'd want taken off our hands. The page doesn't say whether they would.

journey.section: Bringing Nigerian wedding traditions to a wedding in Australia or abroad
journey.quote: Many families choose instead to hold every ceremony in Australia, or at a destination where relatives from Nigeria, the United Kingdom and North America can meet.
journey.reaction: Fine, but this is where I'd expect a word on exclusive use, private transfers and security for a large family gathering. Nothing.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying
journey.quote: Who will gather the notes during spraying, and where will they be kept safe?
journey.reaction: This sounds like someone who has actually run one. Practical, discreet, thinking about security. More of this.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the parts your families lead, as your single point of contact.
journey.reaction: One contact, built around the families. Good. Still nothing on scale or discretion.

journey.section: Planning your Nigerian wedding with us
journey.quote: Nothing is too early or too vague.
journey.reaction: A little eager. It's a door for everyone, not a private conversation.

unanswered_questions: Has Wedded Wonderland delivered a Nigerian or Nigerian-diaspora wedding of 200 to 400 guests, with both a traditional day and a white wedding?
Can they arrange exclusive use of a property for a multi-day traditional and white wedding, closed to the public?
Do they coordinate aso ebi ordering, tailoring and delivery for guests in several countries on the family's behalf?
How do they handle private transfers and work alongside our own security team, including around spraying?
How is privacy protected: vendor NDAs, photography and social media rules for guests?
Can they source an experienced alaga and a Nigerian band or DJ outside Nigeria?
Is there a private or referral channel to someone senior?

turn_offs_found.quote: See [aṣọ-òkè in the V&A collection](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O263819/) for an example of the weave.
turn_offs_found.why: Pointing to museums, Britannica and an academic paper makes the brand sound like a researcher rather than an authority. It undercuts the understated, knowing tone I trust.

turn_offs_found.quote: Nothing is too early or too vague.
turn_offs_found.why: Eager, open-to-anyone phrasing signals a standard client funnel, not a discreet service.

would_share_with: My assistant, to add the aso ebi logistics and spraying security questions to the planner shortlist
The groom's mother, for the Yoruba engagement and alaga sections

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, [speak with a Wedded Advisor](/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=nigerian-wedding-traditions&utm_content=secondary).
cta_reaction.why: Calm, no package or discount talk. But I don't fill in web forms, and nothing here shows they can run a wedding of our size privately. Through my assistant or a referral, possibly.

top_3_changes: Remove the visible sourcing (Britannica, V&A, the journal download link, loom widths) so the voice sounds like a planner who simply knows.

In the 'Bringing Nigerian wedding traditions abroad' section, add one understated line on exclusive use, private transfers, security and coordinating aso ebi for guests in several countries, if that's true.
Replace 'Nothing is too early or too vague' with a quieter line offering a private conversation.
